title: 7 Ways
To Be Liked
credit: Jecker & Landy 1969 · Chartrand & Bargh 1999 · Moreland & Beach 1992 · Aronson 1966 · Byrne 1961 · Huang et al. 2017 · Boothby et al. 2018

lines.text: Some people walk into a room and everyone just likes them.
It looks like magic. It isn't.
Psychologists have studied liking for decades, and a few small moves keep showing up in the research.
Here are seven of them. Every one is backed by a real study, and the last one changes how you'll see every conversation you've ever had.
Number one. Ask for a small favour.
It sounds backwards. Shouldn't you do favours for them?
In 1969, researchers Jon Jecker and David Landy ran a sneaky experiment.
People won money in a study. Afterwards, the researcher asked some of them to give it back, as a personal favour, because he was paying out of his own pocket.
The people who did him that favour ended up liking him more than the people who weren't asked.
It's called the Ben Franklin effect.
Your brain sees itself helping someone, and quietly decides: I must like this person.
So borrow a pen. Ask for their opinion. Small, easy favours.
Number two. Mirror them, quietly.
In 1999, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh had people chat with a partner who was secretly part of the study.
Sometimes the partner copied their posture and movements. Sometimes they didn't.
When they were mimicked, people liked their partner more, and said the conversation flowed more smoothly.
Psychologists call it the chameleon effect.
The key word is quietly. Lean when they lean. Match their energy. Never copy them like a mirror in a cartoon.
Number three. Just keep showing up.
In one study, four women attended a large university lecture.
One came zero times, one came five times, one ten, and one fifteen. They never spoke to anyone.
At the end of term, students were shown their photos.
The more often a woman had been in class, the more the students liked her.
This is the mere exposure effect. Familiar feels safe, and safe feels likeable.
So be around. The regular at the gym, the face at the coffee shop. Familiarity does quiet work.
Number four. Let them see you slip.
In 1966, Elliot Aronson played people recordings of a quiz contestant.
The contestant was brilliant and answered almost everything right.
In one version, at the end, he clumsily spilled coffee all over himself.
Listeners liked the brilliant contestant more after the spill.
It's called the pratfall effect. A small mistake makes a capable person feel human.
It only works if people already see you as competent. So be good at what you do, and don't hide the small slips.
Number five. Find what you share.
Back in 1961, Donn Byrne showed students the opinions of a stranger they'd never met.
The more that stranger's attitudes matched their own, the more they liked them.
Similarity is one of the most reliable findings in the psychology of attraction.
So don't lead with what makes you different. Hunt for the overlap first. Same hometown, same team, same struggle.
Number six. Ask the follow-up question.
In 2017, Harvard researchers studied hundreds of conversations, including speed dates.
People who asked more questions were liked more.
But one type of question did the heavy lifting: the follow-up.
Not, what do you do? But, wait, how did you end up doing that?
A follow-up proves you were actually listening. And being listened to is rare.

lines.chapter: 7. They already like you more than you think
lines.text: And number seven. The one that changes everything.
In 2018, researchers paired strangers for a conversation, then asked two things.
How much do you like your partner? And how much do you think they liked you?
Again and again, people underestimated how much they were liked.
The researchers called it the liking gap.
After a conversation, you replay every awkward moment. The other person mostly remembers that it was nice.
So most of the time, you're already doing better than you think.
Ask for a small favour. Mirror quietly. Keep showing up. Don't hide your slips. Find the overlap. Ask the follow-up. And remember the liking gap.
Try one of these this week, and notice what happens.

post.title: 7 Psychology Tricks That Make People Like You (Backed by Research)
post.description:
Seven small moves that make people like you, and the studies behind them:
• Ben Franklin effect — Jecker & Landy (1969)
• Chameleon effect — Chartrand & Bargh (1999)
• Mere exposure — Moreland & Beach (1992)
• Pratfall effect — Aronson, Willerman & Floyd (1966)
• Similarity — Byrne (1961)
• Follow-up questions — Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017)
• The liking gap — Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018)
